claims.text: The long-term structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and local lattice strain.
High configurational entropy favors retention of a homogeneous phase.
Local lattice strain arising from atomic-size mismatch promotes phase segregation.
Closely matched atomic radii minimize lattice strain in the control nanoparticles.
Introducing 5–10% of an element with a significantly larger atomic radius amplifies local lattice strain.
Atomic-size mismatch induces local lattice distortions and strain fields within the solid solution.
Configurational entropy in near-equiatomic alloys suppresses phase separation.
Sufficient strain caused by atomic-size mismatch can overcome entropic stabilization.
Mismatch-induced lattice strain accelerates atomic diffusion at high temperature.
Accelerated atomic diffusion promotes elemental segregation or phase separation.
Low-strain control nanoparticles will retain a uniform, homogeneous structure under the specified high-temperature conditions.
Nanoparticles with deliberately increased atomic-size mismatch will exhibit more phase segregation than the control.
Nanoparticles with deliberately increased atomic-size mismatch may exhibit selective surface elemental enrichment relative to the control.
Nanoparticles with deliberately increased atomic-size mismatch may develop chemical inhomogeneities relative to the control.
The proposed lattice-strain mechanism is significant primarily between 773 and 1923 K.
At lower temperatures, the effect of lattice strain on stability may be negligible.
When constituent elements have minimal atomic-size differences, the effect of lattice strain on stability may be negligible.
Diffusion coefficients and surface oxidation can influence the quantitative relationship between atomic-size mismatch and segregation kinetics.
